newsitem.title: FRANCE: Nazi-hunter wants police watch on France's Papon.
newsitem.headline: Nazi-hunter wants police watch on France's Papon.

text.p: Nazi-hunter Serge Klarsfeld said on Wednesday that former French cabinet minister Maurice Papon should be placed under police surveillance in case he planned to leave France to avoid trial for crimes against humanity.

An appeals court in Bordeaux last month ordered Papon, 86, to stand trail for sending Jews in wartime France to their deaths in Nazi extermination camps. Papon has appealed against the decision to the Supreme Court.
"I asked the public prosecutor in Bordeaux a few days ago to take away Papon's passport and to put him somewhere under police control," Klarsfeld told the Anglo-American Press Association.
"He is old, has money, and (if he leaves France) he can always say he is ill and cannot be extradited," Klarsfeld added.
He said the request was made on Friday and that the prosecutor had yet to give an answer.
Papon is only the second Frenchman to be sent to trial for crimes against humanity, a charge for which there is no statute of limitations.

The charge was brought onto the books after a statute of limitations prevented new trials for collaboration or war crimes which resulted in tens of thousands of executions and jail terms in immediate post-war years.

Papon, who rose to be Paris police chief in the late 1950s and a Gaullist budget minister in the 1970s before his World War Two role was exposed, is accused of having ordered the deportation of 1,690 Jews, including 223 children, in 1942-44 when he was secretary general of the Bordeaux regional administration.
Most later died at the Auschwitz death camp.

Papon's lawyer has argued that he never followed Nazi ideology and had only obeyed orders. A "jury of honour" accepted in 1981 that Papon joined the Resistance in 1943 but the Bordeaux court concluded this was not proved.
Klarsfeld said he would keep up pressure on the Supreme Court to ensure it rules speedily on whether Papon should stand trial.
"The Supreme Court ruling can take two months or a year. Papon is 86 and we mustn't wait too much. We started the case in 1982 -- 14 years of judicial proceedings is enough," he said.
